summary: Published on April 1st, this humorous RFC proposes the "Two-Week Principle," a supposedly universal scale for estimating how long tasks take. Its joke is that, whatever the task, estimates tend to come out as about two weeks. It is satire about time estimation, not a real protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 9759 is an April 1st joke that says every time estimate should become two weeks. It extends this absurd rule to software, project management, and calendars.

questions: april fools rfc about time estimates
how does twp convert time estimates
subtitle: An April 1st joke maps every time estimate to two weeks.

tldr.problem: This April 1st joke frames time estimation as difficult because people and organizations give inconsistent estimates.
tldr.mechanism: The Two-Week Principle maps every time duration, regardless of its original value, to two weeks.
tldr.outcome: The RFC applies the idea to software, project planning, calendars, and quantum computing in deliberately absurd detail.

today: RFC 9759 is an Informational document published on April 1, 2025. Its Two-Week Principle is a humorous proposal, not a real timekeeping or scheduling standard.

sections.title: The Two-Week Principle
sections.content: RFC 9759 introduces the Two-Week Principle (TWP), a rule stating that any time duration must be converted to two weeks, regardless of its original or intended value. The document presents the rule as a universal response to the difficulty of estimating time.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule says that every duration means two weeks. The document presents this as a solution to time-estimation problems for April 1st.

sections.title: Converting Time Estimates
sections.content: The conversion table maps examples ranging from one second to two years to the same TWP duration. It also maps “ASAP,” “it'll be done when it's done,” and any unlisted time value to two weeks. Each entry shows binary and hexadecimal representations as well.
sections.plainLanguage: A second, a year, and “ASAP” all convert to two weeks under the joke rule. The table gives the same representations for each.

sections.title: Applying the Joke to Software
sections.content: The RFC says software displaying time should replace time values with “two weeks,” project tools should enforce that estimate, and employees should answer time questions that way. It also jokes that iCalendar should normalize meeting and event timestamps to the same duration.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal extends the same answer to software displays, project tools, conversations, and calendars. These instructions are part of the April 1st satire.
